title: Compare The Reviews And Judge Progress
objective: Use actual challenge work and another person’s review to make your own final judgement of progress.

blocks.text: GROW · Art · Trinity Arts Award Silver. Compare The Reviews And Judge Progress.
Objective: Use actual challenge work and another person’s review to make your own final judgement of progress.
Success evidence: Ongoing practice evidence, a real review of the challenge by someone else, the pupil’s own final review and separate exact locations for both reviews.
Use your own artwork, interests and practical choices. You can choose an abstract subject; you do not need to disclose private experiences.
40 minutes. Keep original work before making changes. Ask staff about safe tools and access.

This deck directly serves Silver Unit 1, Part 1B, Implement and review the arts challenge. Silver has TWO units, evidenced separately. This lesson belongs to Unit 1, Arts practice and pathways; keep its evidence labelled by unit and part. ONE Attempted allowed PER UNIT. Any Not Attempted = Below Pass. The whole Silver portfolio has a 20-file cap, not twenty per unit or one new file per lesson. The four assessment areas are art form knowledge and understanding, creativity, planning and review, and communication. Results are Pass or Below Pass only. Only an adviser trained at Silver may assess; delivery is through a validated centre. Staff must confirm those conditions; neither is asserted as completed here. The arts challenge must not focus on leadership. Advisers must not write pupil plans, reviews or evidence. Prompt, read or scribe the pupil’s exact words and check them back unchanged. Core, Extend and Challenge vary support within Silver, retaining the same evidence expectation and the pupil’s own choices. Digital evidence is organised by unit and part, with every locator naming the actual filename plus page, slide or timecode. A portfolio structure is an option, not an extra award rule. Samples, trial counts and prompts here are teaching scaffolds, not qualification quotas. Use accessible tools and communication without forced personal disclosure, compulsory filming or public posting. This forty-minute lesson supports a longer programme of real guided and independent practice; it does not claim all award hours are complete. Source: tools/artsaward/SPEC.json, Silver and universal rules. Part 1B requires ongoing evidence, someone ELSE’s review of the challenge, and the pupil’s own final review. Preserve all three; one cannot substitute for another. The outside reviewer may be a peer, staff member or another appropriate person who can examine the actual challenge evidence; they are not automatically acting as the assessing adviser. Record their identity or role and the location of their genuine review. The pupil makes their own judgement rather than copying or improving that review. A final review may honestly report an unmet artistic aim. If actual practice or a required review is absent, record the gap and arrange completion; a teacher model or generic checklist tick does not fill it. Allow sufficient programme time to complete meaningful practice before the final review.

stages.title: Arrival · retrieve
stages.data-ta1: Check actual process evidence and whether either required review is missing. Arrange a willing reviewer who can examine the work; never supply an invented outside response.

blocks.text: Bring the whole challenge into view
Open your aim, action plan and process record. Put the starting work beside a later state that helps show what happened.
Check that the practice actually took place. A plan and a final picture alone may hide the decisions made between them.
Find the trials, changes and reasons you kept. You will use them to review the challenge rather than rely on memory.
You need two distinct reviews: another person's review of the challenge and your own final review.
A comment about one mark may help. It may not review the whole challenge.
Show the reviewer your aim and work. Listen to their view. Then decide what your own evidence supports.

stages.title: Starter · create the need
stages.data-ta1: Model consistent viewing with actual samples. Do not treat camera exposure, neatness or detail as automatic evidence of artistic improvement.

blocks.text: Progress depends on the intention
Place two versions of a piece where you can view them in the same light. Look from a similar distance and angle.
These simple choices make comparison fairer. A darker photograph does not necessarily mean the artwork gained stronger tone.

For a paper form, view the base and the side, not only the front. If the plan concerned stability, test it on the same flat surface. If it concerned shape, compare the silhouette from the intended view.
Read the original intention before judging the result. A rough texture may serve one purpose, while a smooth transition suits another.
Ask which features changed and whether those changes helped the intended effect. Improvement does not always mean adding detail or making the surface neater.
You may find a strength that grew and a difficulty that remains. Both belong in an honest review.

stages.title: I Do · model
stages.data-ta1: Use real adult-made samples and visibly label the demonstration. Do not distribute the adult’s judgement as a pupil review. Invite evidence-based differences about artistic effect.

blocks.text: Adult model: connect a judgement to work
The adult places their own hatching trials in order. They remind the class of the intended effect before judging the result.
First they look at line spacing. Then they look at where the second layer crosses the first. They point to the actual patches, rather than saying every later patch is better.
They test the view from a little distance. A dark area may draw attention while still keeping a visible line texture.
The adult explains what the work shows and what it cannot show. A preserved sample supports a claim about line quality. It does not prove how long the adult practised unless that time was recorded.
This demonstration models a method of looking and judging. It is not a review written for your portfolio.
Use the same questions with your own art. What was the aim? What actions took place? What effect can be seen?
An outcome may be partly successful. You can explain what worked, what remains uncertain and what you would change next.
Keep the judgement specific to your work. Another maker may prefer a different effect without making your own intention wrong.

blocks.title: A judgement grows from the challenge evidence
blocks.caption: Use the aim, process and outcome to review.
blocks.alt: Four linked boxes connect the original aim, actual process and visible outcome with a reasoned personal review.

stages.title: We Do · everyone commits
stages.data-ta1: A is too general to show a challenge review by itself. B can support the outside review if genuine and located. C is not the pupil’s own review. D can support the pupil’s review if based on real evidence.

blocks.text: Visible review cards: what is still needed?
Choose a card and keep your first answer ready. Point, write or hold its letter. Reveal your choice together, then explain your reason before hearing the adult’s model.
Read these example record types. Decide which could support a real review and which leave something important missing.
The cards are teaching examples, not statements about your own challenge. Explain what you would need to see or hear before accepting the record.
A review need not be long. It must concern the real challenge and give a clear view.

items: A · A general “looks great” comment with no link to the challenge.
B · Another person’s own view of the aim, changes and result, linked to the work.
C · An adult’s completed review copied into the pupil’s section.
D · The pupil’s own judgement of the actual process and outcome, with reasons.

stages.title: I Do 2 · connect
stages.data-ta1: Distinguish an outside review from adviser assessment and from the pupil’s own reflection. Scribe accurately if needed and allow the reviewer to check the record. No compulsory signature or witness-statement format.

blocks.text: Keep two voices distinct
Give the other reviewer enough context to form a fair view. Show your aim, a starting point and useful evidence of the changes.
Ask what progress they notice, what supports their view and what could develop further. Let them reach their own judgement.

Let the reviewer see the work before showing them your preferred judgement. Ask them to point to a detail that supports their view. If they judge a feature you did not intend to change, discuss that difference. It may reveal another possibility without replacing the aim you chose.
They may speak, write or use another agreed format. Keep their actual words or an accurate record they can check. Note who they are or their role.
Now consider your own view. You may agree with part of their review and question another part. Explain your reason through the work.
Do not rewrite their response to make it more positive. Do not copy it and call it your own final review.
Explain the whole challenge. What did you intend? What did you do? What happened? What did you learn from the process?
Keep a separate location for each review, even if they sit in the same part file.

boxes.head: THEIR REVIEW
boxes.line1: another person’s view of my challenge
boxes.line2: identity or role and exact location

boxes.head: MY FINAL REVIEW
boxes.line1: my judgement from the actual evidence
boxes.line2: my reasons and a separate location

blocks.title: Two reviews have different authors
blocks.caption: Keep both voices and locate each review clearly.
blocks.alt: Two panels show the outside reviewer’s own view with attribution and the pupil’s separate final review with their own reasons.

stages.title: We Do 2 · lab
stages.data-ta1: Provide time and access to the real work. Help capture an authentic review; no adult model or checklist tick substitutes for the other person’s view of the challenge.

blocks.text: Ask for the real outside review
Show the challenge evidence to your agreed reviewer. Give a short account of the aim without telling them what they should think.
Let them examine the work and explain their view. Ask a clear follow-up if you need to understand a comment.
Record their review in the agreed way. Read back any notes to check that they represent the review fairly.
If the person cannot review it yet, record that as a next action. A reply you imagine they might give is not evidence.
Keep the reviewer's identity or role with the record. Add the filename and page, slide or timecode so you can return to their actual words.

stages.title: Independent · evidence
stages.data-ta1: Preserve the pupil’s independent judgement. Prompts may organise their response but must not supply their conclusions. All tiers retain actual process evidence and both distinct reviews.

blocks.text: Make your own final review
Return to the original aim and the evidence of your practice. Describe what you actually did, including a choice that changed the work.
Judge the outcome against that aim. Point to what supports your view and acknowledge anything the evidence cannot settle.
Consider the outside review. Explain where it helps you see the work differently, or why your own judgement differs.
Say what you learnt from the process and choose a useful next step. An aim that was not fully met can still teach you something worth explaining.
Use your own words or chosen communication format. If a required element is missing, identify it honestly and arrange completion.
Save your final review under Unit 1, Part 1B. Locate the process evidence, outside review and your own review separately.

items: Core · use prompts and communication support to show the actual challenge work. Gather another person’s real review and make your own final review. Keep the aim, process, outcome, outside view and your judgement clear. Give each review its own exact location.
Extend · make the same complete evidence-based final review in your own format. Compare your view with the other person’s review. Explain agreement or difference. Choose a reasoned next step.
Challenge · keep both real reviews and the full practice record. Look for evidence that suggests different views. Explain any limits in your judgement. Say what another trial could clarify.

stages.title: Exit · Audience and Influence
stages.data-ta1: Check distinct locators for ongoing evidence and both reviews. Only the trained adviser assesses; the lesson checklist does not award a Pass.

blocks.text: Check the evidence behind your judgement
Choose a sentence or spoken point from your own review. Follow its location note back to the work that supports it.
Now find the other person's review. Check that the two voices are clear and that neither record has been changed to sound better.
Tell staff if a real review or piece of practice evidence still needs completing. Keep that action visible.
Your review explains what this challenge taught you. It is evidence for the adviser to assess. It does not promise an award result.

sections: My own final review and next step
print.intro: Gather a real review of the challenge from another person. Use the aim, actual process, outcome and that outside view to make your own final review. Keep both voices separate.
focusRows: What did I intend, what did I do, and what does the work show?
What is the other person’s actual review, and who or what role gave it?
What is my own judgement, including agreement, difference and learning?
Where are the process evidence and both separate reviews?

checks: The review uses actual ongoing practice evidence and the original aim.
Someone else has genuinely reviewed the challenge, with identity or role recorded.
My final review is my own and gives a reasoned judgement of the process and outcome.
The outside review, my judgement and any remaining gaps are distinguished honestly.
Process evidence and both reviews are separately located by filename plus page, slide or timecode under Unit 1, Part 1B.
